system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2154-03-02 15:07:00 to 2154-03-09 15:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with chronic pancreatitis, depression, anxiety, and a history of C. difficile and venous thrombosis, was admitted with severe mid-epigastric abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, consistent with a flare of her chronic pancreatitis. She was found to be hypovolemic, with stable mental status and no evidence of C. difficile infection. IV access was difficult, requiring midline placement. She was managed with IV fluids, Dilaudid, promethazine, and Toradol initially, then transitioned to oral tramadol and home medications as her condition improved. Hypertension was managed by holding hydrochlorothiazide initially and starting lisinopril. She tolerated a soft diet, was weaned off IV narcotics, and discharged home in stable condition with all home medications, including Creon, amitriptyline, quetiapine, and omeprazole, and instructions to follow up with her primary care provider.
problems: Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with chronic pancreatitis and difficult access,
history of PICC lines placed by ___  // Please place a PICC line

COMPARISON:  PICC line placement from ___.

TECHNIQUE:   OPERATORS: Dr. ___ radiology fellow) and Dr.
___ radiology attending) performed the procedure.  The
attending, Dr. ___ was present and supervising throughout the procedure.
Dr. ___ radiologist, personally supervised the trainee during
the key components of the procedure and reviewed and agreed with the trainee's
findings.
ANESTHESIA: 1% lidocaine was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues
overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: 1% lidocaine.
CONTRAST: None.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  9.8 minutes, 136 cGy-cm2

PROCEDURE:
1. Single lumen PICC placement through the brachial vein on the right.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the brachial
vein on the right was punctured under direct ultrasound guidance using a
micropuncture set. Permanent ultrasound images were obtained before and after
intravenous access, which confirmed vein patency. A peel-away sheath was then
placed over a guidewire.  Attempts to advance the guidewire were met with
resistance at the level of the axillary vein/distal subclavian vein. After
speaking with the primary team, the decision was made to leave a midline
catheter. A single lumen PIC line measuring 16 cm in length was then placed
through the peel-away sheath with its tip positioned in the axillary vein
under fluoroscopic guidance. Position of the catheter was confirmed by a
fluoroscopic spot film of the chest. The peel-away sheath and guidewire were
then removed. The catheter was secured to the skin, flushed, and a sterile
dressing applied.

The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  The accessed vein was patent and compressible.
2.  Brachialvein approach single lumen right PICC with tip in the axillary
vein.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a right 16 cm brachial approach single lumen Power
PICC (MIDLINE) with tip in the axillary vein.  The line is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You’re here for abdominal pain—can you tell me about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s that same pain I always get—around my belly button, going to my back. Nausea and vomiting too. Feels like my usual pancreatitis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That matches what we saw in the ER. You’ve had this before, and we know it’s tough. You said you haven’t had alcohol or drugs—good. We’ll focus on managing the pain and getting fluids in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just can’t get an IV. They kept trying in the ER and couldn’t get one. I had to get shots instead. It’s frustrating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Your chart says you’ve had trouble with IV access before. The team tried again, but it didn’t work. We’ve called Interventional Radiology to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are they going to try another IV? I don’t want more shots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll try to place a midline—a longer IV that goes into a bigger vein in your arm. It should last for this stay and let us give you fluids and meds smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better. When will they do it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re scheduling it for tomorrow morning. For now, we’ll keep giving pain meds and anti-nausea medicine by injection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on 7 out of 10 for pain. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s significant, but your exam shows your belly is soft, no serious tenderness. That means we can manage it safely with meds. We’ll keep adjusting until you’re more comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve been so sick I haven’t eaten. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now. It helps your pancreas rest. Once the pain improves, we’ll start you on clear liquids and work up to food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my Creon? Should I take that when I eat again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Once you’re on solid food, you’ll restart Creon with meals. It helps you digest properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The radiology team just placed your midline in the right arm. It’s in the axillary vein, so it’s secure and ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, great! Did it work okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they had some trouble advancing the wire, so they decided on a midline instead of a PICC. But it’s perfect for your needs—fluids, meds, no more injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I move my arm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but gently. Avoid heavy lifting. The nurse will show you how to care for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Your lipase was only 41—low for pancreatitis—so this is likely a flare of chronic disease, not a new acute attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I feel so sick. How can the numbers be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your symptoms can be severe even if the lab markers aren’t sky-high. Your history of chronic pancreatitis explains that. We’re treating it the same way—rest, fluids, pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my liver tests? I saw they were high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ALT, AST, and alkaline phosphatase are mildly elevated. It’s common with pancreatitis. We’ll watch them, but nothing suggests a liver problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. Pain is down to 4, and you’re not nauseous. We’re going to try a clear liquid diet this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I haven’t had anything to drink in days. Can I have apple juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with water, broth, and clear juices like apple juice. If you tolerate it, we’ll advance to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope I can keep it down. Last time I tried too soon and threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. If you have any nausea, let the nurse know right away. We can give promethazine if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you kept down the clear liquids. Today, we’re starting a soft diet: mashed potatoes, toast, things like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’m so hungry. Can I have more later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see how you do. If you tolerate this, we can move to regular food tomorrow. And we’ll start transitioning your pain meds from IV to oral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Dilaudid. Are you switching me back to tramadol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart your home tramadol for pain. We’ll keep IV meds available if you need a boost, but the goal is to get you off IV narcotics before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been high—around 150–160 over 90. You’re on lisinopril, but we’re adding amlodipine to help control it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’ve had heart issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, amlodipine is safe for you. Your heart function has improved—your EF is now over 50%. This med will help protect your heart and kidneys long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool for C. diff because of your history. The result came back negative, which is great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about that. I’ve had it before and it was awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But this time, it’s not the cause of your nausea. Your symptoms are from the pancreatitis flare, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on a regular diet all day and doing well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if everything stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. What do I need to do after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your home meds: Creon with meals, amitriptyline, quetiapine, omeprazole, and now amlodipine for blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And tramadol for pain if I need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, tramadol as needed. But try to use it sparingly. We want to avoid long-term narcotic use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Should I follow up with my doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, schedule an appointment within a week. And if your pain worsens or you can’t keep food down, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night you slept well, pain was 2, and you ate breakfast without issues. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What about the midline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll remove it before you leave. It’s done its job. No need to keep it once you’re on oral meds and eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mental health? I’ve been feeling okay, but it’s been a rough few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad you’re feeling stable. You’re on lamotrigine and quetiapine, which are helping. Keep in touch with your psychiatrist. If you feel low or anxious, don’t wait—reach out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The midline is out, and you’ve had a light lunch. All set. I’ll sign your discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Remember: take your meds, eat small meals, and follow up. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m ready to get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check-in. You’re officially discharged. Your condition is stable, alert, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you hopefully never, but I know where to go if I need to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Stay well.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with chronic pancreatitis, depression, anxiety, and a history of venous thrombosis and C. difficile, was readmitted with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting consistent with an acute flare of her chronic pancreatitis. She had difficulty with IV access, requiring a midline catheter placement after failed PICC attempts. She was managed with IV fluids, analgesics, and antiemetics, then transitioned to oral tramadol and a regular diet as her symptoms improved. Her lipase was normal, and stool testing ruled out C. difficile. Hypertension was managed with lisinopril and the addition of amlodipine. She remained mentally stable, tolerated discharge on a regular diet, and was sent home with all home medications and follow-up instructions.
